lessons.title: Recording Studio Equipment & Safety
lessons.description: Microphones, DI, audio interfaces, monitoring and health and safety in the studio.
lessons.content_html:
Recording Studio Equipment

A recording studio is a controlled environment designed to capture high-quality audio. Understanding the equipment in a studio — and how to use it safely — is essential for anyone working in music technology. This lesson covers the core equipment you need to know for the exam.

Microphones

Microphones convert sound waves into electrical signals. There are two main types you must know:

Dynamic microphones use a moving coil attached to a diaphragm. They are robust, do not require external power, and handle loud volumes well. They are ideal for live performance and recording loud sources like drums and guitar amplifiers.

Condenser microphones use an electrically charged diaphragm. They are more sensitive than dynamic microphones and capture greater detail and nuance. They require phantom power (48V) to operate and are best suited for studio vocals, acoustic instruments, and room ambience.

A microphone’s polar pattern describes the directions from which it picks up sound. A cardioid pattern picks up mainly from the front, rejecting sound from the sides and rear — useful for isolating a single source. An omnidirectional pattern picks up equally from all directions — useful for room ambience. A figure-of-eight pattern picks up from the front and rear but rejects the sides — useful for recording two facing sources simultaneously.

A microphone’s frequency response shows how it responds to different frequencies. A flat frequency response means the microphone treats all frequencies equally, reproducing sound accurately. Some microphones have a “presence peak” — a boost in the upper frequencies that adds brightness to vocals.

Key Fact

Dynamic microphones: robust, no external power needed, handle loud sources. Condenser microphones: more sensitive, capture detail, require 48V phantom power. Choose dynamic for live/loud sources, condenser for studio/detailed recordings.

DI (Direct Injection)

A DI box (Direct Injection box) is used to connect instruments like electric guitars, bass guitars, and keyboards directly to a mixing desk or audio interface. The DI box performs level matching — it converts the instrument’s high-impedance, unbalanced signal into a low-impedance, balanced signal. This reduces noise and allows the signal to travel over long cable runs without quality loss.

Audio Interfaces

An audio interface is the bridge between the analogue world (microphones, instruments) and the digital world (the computer and DAW). Key features include:

  • Phantom power — 48V supply for condenser microphones, activated per channel.
  • Balanced and unbalanced inputs — balanced inputs (XLR or TRS) reject interference; unbalanced inputs (standard jack) are for shorter cable runs.
  • Pre-amps — built-in preamplifiers boost the weak microphone signal to a usable level.
  • Outputs — connections for speakers (monitors) and headphones.
  • DAW connectivity — the interface connects to the computer via USB, Thunderbolt, or similar connection.

Multitrack Recorder & Recording Processes

A multitrack recorder can be hardware (a standalone unit) or software (a DAW on a computer). It records multiple audio signals on separate tracks so each instrument or voice can be edited and mixed independently.

The recording process involves several stages: selecting the correct input source (microphone or DI), mic placement (close-mic for isolation, room-mic for ambience), gain optimisation (setting the input level so the signal is strong but does not clip or distort), and overdubbing (recording additional parts on new tracks while listening back to previously recorded tracks).

Additional Equipment & Monitoring

Studios also require: stands (mic stands, boom stands), cables (XLR, jack, speaker), connectors (XLR, 6.35mm jack, 3.5mm jack), pop shields (mesh screens that reduce plosive sounds from vocals), cases (protective storage), and rack units (outboard processors mounted in standard 19-inch racks).

The studio is divided into two spaces: the control room (where the engineer works, with speakers and the mixing desk) and the live room (where the performer records, acoustically treated to control reflections). Speakers (studio monitors) provide accurate, flat-response playback in the control room. Headphones allow the performer in the live room to hear the backing track while recording. Talkback is an intercom system that lets the engineer communicate with the performer in the live room.

Health & Safety in the Recording Studio

Health and safety is a legal and practical requirement. You must understand the hazards, risks, and control measures for a recording studio environment.

Key Fact

Hazards and risks: Noise → hearing loss. Displays (screens) → eye strain. Slip/trip/fall (cables on the floor, equipment) → sprains and injuries. Electrical (faulty equipment, liquids near electronics) → electrocution. A risk assessment must be carried out before every session, and control measures (e.g. cable management, volume limits, PAT testing) must be in place. Incidents and near-misses must be reported.

Key Fact

Control measures: For noise — set volume limits, use hearing protection. For displays — take regular breaks, adjust screen brightness. For slip/trip/fall — tape cables to the floor, keep walkways clear. For electrical — use PAT-tested equipment, keep liquids away from electronics. Always complete a risk assessment and know the reporting procedure for incidents.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Health and safety questions appear regularly. Always structure your answer around: identify the hazard, state the risk, and describe the control measure. For equipment questions, explain why a piece of equipment is used, not just what it is — for example, “phantom power is needed because condenser microphones require a 48V supply to charge their diaphragm.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Dynamic microphones are robust and handle loud sources; condenser microphones are sensitive, detailed, and require 48V phantom power.
  • An audio interface converts analogue signals to digital and provides phantom power, pre-amps, inputs, outputs, and DAW connectivity.
  • Studio health and safety covers four main hazards (noise, displays, slip/trip/fall, electrical) with corresponding risks, control measures, risk assessment, and reporting.

practice_questions.marks: Award marks for explanation with reasoning (max 4): Gain optimisation means setting the input level so the signal is strong enough to record clearly (1) but does not clip or distort (1). practice_questions.text: Analyse the health and safety considerations a recording engineer must address before and during a studio session. Refer to specific hazards, risks, and control measures.

Before the session: conduct a risk assessment, check equipment is PAT tested, tape cables down. Noise: prolonged exposure to loud monitors causes hearing loss — set volume limits, use hearing protection. Electrical: faulty equipment could cause electrocution — check cables, keep liquids away. Slips/trips: cables on the floor cause falls — use cable management. Displays: prolonged screen use causes eye strain — take regular breaks.
Mid band (3-4): Some hazards identified with risks and control measures but less detailed.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements about safety with limited specific hazards or measures.

practice_questions.text: You are setting up a recording session for a four-piece band (vocals, electric guitar, bass guitar, and drums). Discuss the equipment you would need and the choices you would make for microphone selection, DI, and monitoring. Justify your decisions.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Comprehensive discussion covering all four instruments with justified equipment choices. E.g. Vocals: condenser mic (cardioid) for detail, pop shield, phantom power from interface. Guitar amp: dynamic mic (cardioid) close-miked — handles loud volumes. Bass: DI box for clean signal direct to interface, with level matching. Drums: combination of dynamic mics (kick, snare) and condensers (overheads). Monitoring: headphones for all performers in the live room, studio monitors in the control room, talkback for communication. Audio interface with sufficient inputs and pre-amps.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good discussion covering most instruments with some justification.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some valid equipment choices but limited justification or missing instruments.
Lower band (1-2): Basic equipment list with little or no justification.

lessons.title: Planning & Undertaking Multitrack Recordings
lessons.description: Roles, planning, setup, gain optimisation, overdubbing and file management.
lessons.content_html:
Planning a Recording Session

A successful multitrack recording does not start when the red light goes on — it starts with careful planning. Before any microphone is positioned or any cable is connected, the recording team must agree on roles, timelines, goals, and requirements. Poor planning leads to wasted studio time, frustrated artists, and poor-quality recordings.

Roles in the Studio

Three key roles are involved in a recording session:

The artist is the musician or singer being recorded. They perform the parts and may have specific preferences about monitoring, headphone mix, and studio setup.

The engineer operates the recording equipment. They set up microphones, manage the audio interface and DAW, optimise gain levels, monitor audio quality, and handle all technical aspects of the session.

The producer takes the creative lead. They guide the artistic direction of the recording, make decisions about arrangement, performance quality, and overall sound. In some sessions, the engineer and producer may be the same person.

Key Fact

The three key studio roles are: Artist (performs the music), Engineer (operates equipment and manages the technical side), and Producer (guides the creative direction and makes artistic decisions).

Planning Elements

Before a recording session, several planning elements must be agreed:

  • Time constraints and timeline — when does the recording need to be finished? Working backwards from the deadline helps allocate time for recording, editing, and mixing.
  • Session length — how many hours are booked? Sessions must be realistic — booking too little time creates pressure, while booking too much wastes budget.
  • Agreed goals — what needs to be achieved in this session? For example: “Record drums and bass for three songs” or “Capture lead vocals for the single.”
  • Hardware and software requirements — what equipment is needed? Are specific microphones, instruments, amplifiers, or software plug-ins required?
  • Artist requirements — does the artist need a specific headphone mix, lyric sheets, a particular room setup, or breaks at set intervals?

Without clear planning, sessions often run into problems: the wrong microphone is booked and has to be substituted at the last minute; the session overruns because goals were unrealistic; the artist is uncomfortable because their requirements were not discussed in advance; or the engineer wastes time searching for the right cable because the equipment list was not checked. Each of these issues costs time and money, and reduces the quality of the final recording.

Setting Up for Recording

Once planning is complete, the engineer sets up the studio. This involves selecting and positioning microphones, connecting cables, routing signals to the audio interface, and creating a new project in the DAW with correctly labelled tracks.

Testing is essential before the session begins. The engineer checks every microphone, cable, and input to confirm the signal is reaching the DAW correctly. They listen for noise, hum, or faulty connections and fix any issues before the artist arrives or begins performing.

Appropriate use of equipment means using each item for its intended purpose — for example, not running a condenser microphone without phantom power, or not plugging an instrument into a microphone input without a DI box.

Health and safety measures must be in place: cables taped down, volume limits set, risk assessment completed, and emergency exits clear.

Gain Optimisation

Gain optimisation is one of the most important technical skills in recording. The engineer adjusts the gain (input level) on the audio interface or pre-amp so that the signal is loud enough to produce a clean recording, but not so loud that it clips (distorts). The target is to have peaks reaching around −6 dB to −12 dB on the meter, leaving headroom for unexpected loud moments.

Monitoring During Recording

Monitoring means listening to the audio during and after recording. The engineer monitors through studio speakers or headphones in the control room, checking levels, quality, and balance. The artist wears headphones in the live room to hear a mix of the backing track and their own performance. The headphone mix the artist hears should be comfortable — if they cannot hear themselves clearly, their performance will suffer.

Overdubbing

Overdubbing is the process of recording additional parts on new tracks while playing back previously recorded material. For example, a band might record drums first, then overdub bass, then guitars, then vocals. Each part gets its own track, allowing independent editing and mixing later. The engineer must monitor for timing issues, check gain on each new track, and ensure the artist’s headphone mix is updated for each overdub.

Key Fact

The five planning elements are: time constraints/timeline, session length, agreed goals, hardware/software requirements, and artist requirements. These must all be confirmed before the session begins.

File Management

Good file management prevents lost work and confusion. Three rules apply:

  • Naming audio files — each recorded take should have a clear, descriptive name (e.g. “LeadVocal_Take03.wav” rather than “Audio_001”).
  • Labelling folders — audio files should be organised into folders by song, instrument, or session date.
  • Naming projects — the DAW project file itself should have a clear name that includes the song title and date (e.g. “SunriseDemo_2026-03-30”).

Always save the project at regular intervals and create backups. Use “Save As” with a new version number when making significant changes (e.g. “SunriseDemo_v2”). Keep all audio files within the project folder so the DAW can always find them. If files are moved or renamed outside the DAW, the project may lose its links and audio will go missing.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about planning, always link each planning element to a practical reason. For example, do not just write “you need to plan session length” — explain why: “Session length must be planned so there is enough time to record all parts without rushing, which would affect performance quality.” For file management questions, give specific examples of good naming conventions.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Three key roles in a recording session are the artist, engineer, and producer — each with distinct responsibilities.
  • Planning covers time constraints, session length, agreed goals, hardware/software requirements, and artist requirements.
  • Good file management (naming files, labelling folders, naming projects) prevents lost work and keeps sessions organised.

lessons.title: Mixing & Stereo Mixdowns
lessons.description: Balance, EQ, effects, dynamics, automation, monitoring and exporting stereo mixes.
lessons.content_html:
The Mixing Process

Once all parts have been recorded, the next stage is mixing. Mixing is where raw multitrack recordings are transformed into a polished, professional-sounding piece of music. The engineer adjusts volume, panning, EQ, effects, and dynamics on every track to create a balanced, engaging final mix. This lesson covers all the mixing concepts and tools you need for the exam.

Balance & the Stereo Field

Relative volume is the starting point of any mix. The engineer adjusts the faders so that each instrument sits at the right level — vocals are typically the loudest element in a pop mix, with drums and bass providing the foundation, and other instruments filling in around them.

The stereo field is the space between the left and right speakers. Sounds can be placed anywhere across this field using panning controls. Placing instruments in different positions across the stereo field creates width and separation, preventing a cluttered, mono-sounding mix.

Soundstage Placement

A good mix creates a three-dimensional soundstage — the illusion that the listener is hearing a real performance in a physical space. The soundstage has three dimensions:

Height is controlled by frequency and timbre. Bass-heavy instruments (kick drum, bass guitar) sit at the bottom of the soundstage, while bright instruments (cymbals, high synths) sit at the top. The ear naturally perceives high frequencies as “higher” and low frequencies as “lower.”

Width is controlled by stereo placement, panning, and the stereo image. Panning an instrument hard left or hard right pushes it to the edge of the stereo field. Keeping lead vocals and bass in the centre provides a solid anchor. Spreading guitars, keyboards, and backing vocals across the field creates width.

Depth is controlled by ambience (using delay and reverb) and dynamic processing. A sound with lots of reverb appears further away. A dry, close-miked sound appears right in front of the listener. Adjusting the balance of dry signal versus reverb/delay controls how near or far each element sounds.

Key Fact

The three dimensions of a soundstage are: Height (controlled by frequency and timbre), Width (controlled by stereo placement, panning, and stereo image), and Depth (controlled by ambience — reverb and delay — and dynamic processing).

Corrective Editing

Before applying creative effects, the engineer may need to fix problems in the recordings:

  • Unwanted audio removal — deleting coughs, chair creaks, count-ins, or background noise between phrases.
  • Pitch correction — using tools like auto-tune to fix slightly out-of-tune notes in a vocal or instrument performance.
  • Rhythmic correction — nudging audio clips or quantising MIDI notes so that timing is tight and consistent.

EQ (Equalisation)

EQ shapes the tonal character of each track. Key EQ controls include:

  • Low-pass filter — removes frequencies above a set point, keeping only the low end.
  • High-pass filter — removes frequencies below a set point, keeping only the high end. Commonly used to cut rumble from vocal tracks.
  • Frequency selection — choosing which specific frequency to boost or cut.
  • Q — the width of the frequency band being affected. A narrow Q targets a precise frequency; a wide Q affects a broad range.
  • Gain — how much the selected frequency is boosted.
  • Attenuation — how much the selected frequency is cut (reduced).

Effects

Effects add character, space, and interest to a mix. You must know the following:

Reverb simulates the reflections of a room. Delay creates repeating echoes. Chorus thickens a sound by doubling it with slight pitch and timing variations. Flanging creates a sweeping, jet-like effect. Phasing produces a similar sweeping effect by cancelling certain frequencies. Wah-wah sweeps a filter to mimic a human vocal sound. Amp sim (amplifier simulation) recreates the sound of a guitar amplifier digitally. Overdrive adds harmonic distortion for warmth or aggression.

Dynamics Processing

Dynamics processors control the volume range of a signal. Three types are essential:

A compressor reduces the volume of audio that exceeds a set threshold. The ratio controls how much reduction is applied (e.g. 4:1 means for every 4 dB over the threshold, only 1 dB passes through). Attack controls how quickly compression starts. Release controls how quickly it stops. Gain (make-up gain) compensates for the volume lost during compression.

A limiter is a compressor with an extreme ratio (typically infinity:1). It prevents any audio from exceeding the threshold, acting as a hard ceiling. Limiters are used on the master bus to prevent clipping.

A gate works in reverse — it silences audio that falls below the threshold. Gates are used to remove background noise, headphone bleed, or room ambience between drum hits or vocal phrases.

Key Fact

The five compressor parameters are: Threshold (level at which compression begins), Ratio (amount of reduction, e.g. 4:1), Attack (how quickly compression starts), Release (how quickly it stops), and Gain (make-up gain to restore lost volume).

Connections, Automation & Monitoring

Inserts place an effect directly in the signal path of a single track (e.g. EQ and compressor on a vocal). Auxiliaries (bus sends) route a copy of the signal to a shared effect — pre-fade sends are independent of the fader (used for headphone monitoring), while post-fade sends follow the fader level (used for shared reverb/delay). Routing is the path audio follows through the mixer from input to output.

Automation records changes to volume, panning, or effect sends over time, so adjustments play back automatically. For example, the engineer might automate a vocal volume boost during the chorus, or gradually increase reverb send during a fade-out.

Monitoring during mixing uses headphones for detail checks, main speakers (large monitors) for full-range listening, and near-field speakers (smaller monitors) that simulate a typical listening environment. The engineer also checks the mix against reference material — a professionally mixed track in a similar style — to judge tonal balance and loudness.

Stereo Mixdowns & Export

The final step is creating a stereo mixdown — bouncing all tracks into a single stereo audio file. The engineer can also export individual stems (groups of tracks, e.g. all drums, all vocals) for further processing or remixing.

Key Fact

When exporting a stereo mixdown, you must choose: Bit depth (e.g. 16-bit for CD, 24-bit for professional), Sample rate (e.g. 44.1 kHz for CD, 48 kHz for video), and Format (WAV or AIF for lossless, MP3 for compressed). Higher bit depth and sample rate mean better quality but larger file sizes.

Bit depth determines the dynamic range of the recording — how much difference there is between the quietest and loudest sounds. 16-bit provides 96 dB of dynamic range (CD standard). 24-bit provides 144 dB (professional standard). Sample rate determines how many times per second the audio signal is measured. 44.1 kHz is the CD standard (44,100 samples per second). 48 kHz is common for video work. Higher sample rates capture more high-frequency detail.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Extended response questions about mixing often ask you to describe how you would mix a specific scenario. Structure your answer around the mixing stages: balance (volume and panning), corrective editing, EQ, effects, dynamics, automation, and monitoring. For dynamics questions, always state the five compressor parameters and explain what each one does. Use the correct terminology — “threshold” not “level,” “ratio” not “amount.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A mix creates a three-dimensional soundstage using height (frequency), width (stereo panning), and depth (reverb/delay).
  • Key mixing tools include EQ (frequency shaping), effects (reverb, delay, chorus, etc.), and dynamics processors (compressor, limiter, gate) with five parameters: threshold, ratio, attack, release, and gain.
  • Stereo mixdowns are exported with a chosen bit depth, sample rate, and format (WAV, AIF, or MP3).

practice_questions.text:
Which dynamics processor prevents audio from exceeding a set level by applying an extreme compression ratio?
A) Compressor
B) Gate
C) Limiter
D) EQ
practice_questions.marks: C — Limiter (1 mark). A limiter uses an extreme ratio (typically infinity:1) to prevent audio from exceeding the threshold.

practice_questions.text: Identify two effects that create a sense of depth in a mix.
Describe the three dimensions of a soundstage and explain what controls each one.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per valid point (max 3): Height is controlled by frequency and timbre (1). Width is controlled by stereo placement/panning (1). Depth is controlled by ambience — reverb and delay (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a compressor works, referring to threshold, ratio, attack, and release.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for explanation (max 4): A compressor reduces the volume of audio exceeding the threshold (1). Ratio determines how much reduction — e.g. 4:1 means 4 dB over becomes 1 dB over (1). Attack controls how quickly compression starts after the signal exceeds the threshold (1). Release controls how quickly compression stops after the signal drops below the threshold (1). Make-up gain restores lost volume (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse the difference between using inserts and auxiliary sends when adding effects in a mix. Explain when each approach is most appropriate.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed analysis of both routing methods with clear application. E.g. Inserts place an effect directly in the signal chain of a single track — suitable for EQ and compression which are unique to each track. Aux sends route a copy to a shared effect bus — suitable for reverb and delay where multiple tracks share the same effect, saving CPU and creating a cohesive space. Post-fade sends follow the track fader, so reverb tails disappear naturally when the track is faded down. Pre-fade sends are independent — used for headphone monitoring mixes.
Mid band (3-4): Some valid points about both methods with less detailed application.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements about inserts or sends with limited understanding.

practice_questions.text: You have finished recording a band and are ready to mix the multitrack session. Discuss the steps you would take to create a professional stereo mixdown, from initial balance through to the final export. Include references to EQ, effects, dynamics, automation, monitoring, and export settings.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Comprehensive, well-structured discussion covering the full mixing workflow. E.g. Start with rough balance — set relative volumes, pan instruments across the stereo field. Corrective editing: remove unwanted noise, fix timing/pitch issues. EQ: high-pass filter on vocals to remove rumble, cut/boost frequencies for clarity. Effects: reverb on vocals and snare for depth, delay on guitar for interest. Dynamics: compress vocals for even level, gate drums to remove bleed, limiter on master bus. Automation: boost vocal in chorus, fade reverb at the end. Monitoring: check on near-field speakers, headphones, and against reference material. Export: bounce to stereo WAV at 24-bit/48 kHz, plus MP3 for client preview.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good discussion covering most stages with some specifics.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some valid points but incomplete coverage of the mixing process.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements about mixing with little structure or specificity.

glossary_terms.definition: The process of combining and balancing multiple recorded tracks into a final stereo or surround sound output.
The left-to-right space between the two speakers in a stereo system, within which sounds can be positioned using panning.
The perceived three-dimensional space of a mix, described in terms of height (frequency), width (stereo placement), and depth (ambience).
Equalisation — an audio processing tool that boosts or cuts specific frequency ranges to shape the tonal character of a sound.
Audio processing tools that control the volume range of a signal, including compressors, limiters, and gates.
A dynamics processor that reduces the volume of audio that exceeds a set threshold, evening out the dynamic range.
A dynamics processor that silences audio below a set threshold, used to remove background noise or bleed between loud passages.
Recorded parameter changes that play back automatically during mixing, such as volume, panning, or effect send adjustments over time.
The process of combining all tracks in a multitrack project into a single stereo audio file for distribution.
